Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod # Chapter 3 Production and Industry Trends ## 3.1 Overview #### **Introduction and content** This chapter reviews copper wirerod production trends and industry developments. We present national and world production data for the period 2000-2007, along with company production estimates for 2005, 2006 and 2007. Production forecasts for the period 2008-2012 are detailed in **Chapter 4 – Market Forecast** . This chapter draws upon a detailed survey that we conducted of all copper wirerod manufacturers with an output of more than 50,000tpy. We also surveyed a number of smaller producers and conducted fieldwork in Europe, China, South Korea and Taiwan, the Gulf States and North Africa. Our production series utilises published industry and government statistics (where considered reliable and wholly representative), as well as our own analysis of less well documented national markets through fieldwork visits, detailed analysis of export/import trade flows, refined copper consumption trends, company financial reports, news and press releases. CRU welcomes feedback on our statistics and company production estimates and rankings. #### **Main Findings** - **World production of copper wirerod grew from 11.3m tonnes in 2000 to 14.2m tonnes in 2007 at a compound annual growth rate of 3.3%.** - **2004 was the strongest year for growth with an impressive 8.8% expansion resulting from an unprecedented synchronised expansion in every major region.** - **2006 and 2007 were years of above average growth, with back to back increases of 3.7% and 4.9% respectively. This alone added 1.14m tonnes to world output.** - **Wirerod production from direct use scrap grew by 93% from 641kt to 1,238kt between 2000-2007. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Chapter 3 Production & Industry Trends 3 - 13 ## 3.2 Production by Region #### 3.2.1 North America **Canadian** production had been on an upward trend since the recession of 2001. Output peaked at 275,000 tonnes in the boom year of 2004 but remained close to this level in the subsequent two years. However 2007 was an altogether different proposition – a reasonable first half was followed by a catastrophic collapse in the second half as the US sub prime triggered recession took hold. Canadian wirerod production has become increasingly reliant upon export sales to the US as the Canadian wire and cable industry has withered following a spate of closures and rationalisation measures. The strength of the Canadian dollar has proved detrimental to the health of the domestic wire and cable industry, stifling exports to the neighbouring US market but attracting imports, and thereby undermining production volumes and the profitability of the industry. The same has been true of the wirerod and drawn wire business which saw exports plummet 26% in 2007 from 190,000 tonnes to 140,000 tonnes as US sales slumped. At the same time wirerod imports surged 18% from 52,000 tonnes to 62,000 tonnes placing the Canadian wirerod industry under tremendous pressure. As a consequence Canadian wirerod production plummeted by 68,000 tonnes, or 25%, in 2007 to 203,000 tonnes. The Canadian wirerod industry is comprised of only two mills. The smallest of these is Electrical Components International (formerly the Noma Corporation until 2007) which operates a small Outokumpu mill with a capacity of around 10,000tpy in Toronto almost exclusively for internal use. Production has been running close to capacity in recent years. However, the dominant player in the industry has been Ne

xans which has been operating its giant Contirod mill in Montreal since 1982.  Nexans has increasingly become a company that has “ _fallen out of love with copper_ ” since the copper price rally began (see European section). Group policy has shifted to emphasise growth of their insulated wire and cable business (especially in developing economies) and to shrink their electrical wire business unit.  This led to the sale of their global winding wire business to Superior Essex (subsequently acquired by LS Cable).  Nexans also has a deliberate policy of only manufacturing wirerod for internal group use (or only for external sale if the customer purchases cathode) to avoid tying up financial resources in working capital for profitability levels much lower than those achievable in their insulated wire and cable business.  In this regard Nexans’ Montreal wirerod facility is the most exposed, as the group’s insulated wire and cable manufacturing footprint in Canada and the United States is fairly limited and there are only limited viable opportunities for export to the Caribbean and Central America.  Nexans also lost their anti-dumping appeal against imports of wirerod from Russia so there is no prospect of reprieve on this issue. 

In conclusion, we are not very optimistic about the continued future of the Nexans Montreal mill.  2008 has already seen the onset of a severe recession in the North American wire and cable industry and this is unlikely to abate any time soon.  The general economic climate is deteriorating and faced with inflationary pressures the scope for a rebound is limited. Meanwhile the Canadian dollar will remain uncompetitive against the US dollar undermining the trade balance in wirerod and drawn wire, as well as the outlook for the Canadian insulated wire and cable business.  Faced with these prospects and stated group policy we feel that Nexans will be unwilling to continue to operate the mill sub-optimally for a prolonged period. If a buyer cannot be found then we believe that Nexans will announce the closure of the mill.

Wirerod production in the **United States** reached its peak between 1998 and 2000 when output totalled in excess of 2.1 million tonnes per year.  The recession that followed saw production fall in the three successive years to a low of 1.65 million tonnes in 2003.  A short lived recovery followed in 2004 before the downward trend re-emerged in 2005 and 2006.  2007 posted no recovery, merely a reprieve before economic reality caught up with the North American wire and cable industry which the US wirerod industry serves.  The sudden and severe deterioration in the second quarter of 2008 has confirmed that more tough times are ahead. 

A great deal has changed in the US wirerod industry over the past decade.  At the start of the period demand from the domestic wire and cable industry was fairly healthy and the chief threat to the rod industry came from competitively priced imports from neighbouring Canada and Mexico.  Imports from Mexico were significant in 2000 and 2001 before dwindling as the US recession took hold.  They rebounded in 2005, however the recovery was short lived as the weakness of the US dollar rapidly choked off import growth.  Imports from Canada, particularly into the North Eastern states, have been a perennial feature of the American rod and drawn wire market, never accounting for less than 100,000tpy.  These advanced rapidly between 20042006, seemingly heading towards 200,000 tpy, as the US wire and cable industry recovered on the back of the house building boom and economic upswing.  This coincided with the decisions by General Cable and Asarco to cease rod production in the US, it was a natural opportunity for Mexican and Canadian exporters to sell more to US customers.  At the time exchange rates were more favourable than they are today.  The rationalisation and closure of large parts of the Canadian wire and cable industry also meant that Nexans needed more export business to offset its lower domestic shipments. 

The main issue that has come to dominate the US wirerod market has been the tidal wave of Russian rod exports (See Russia section).  Competitively priced imports of rod from Russia, of acceptable quality for energy cable applications, swamped the US market in 2005 and 2006.  It was only with the application of additional duties, the swift depreciation of the US dollar and the slowdown in US wire and cable industry that this was trend was reduced to manageable proportions in 2007.  Thereafter the flow of trade stopped completely as Russian mills and traders switched target to the Middle East and North Africa.  However, Russian imports

es open to US rod mills. 

Mexico, and to a lesser extent Canada and Central America\Caribbean also present attractive export markets for rod and drawn wire from the US rod industry, especially at prevailing exchange rate levels.  The USA is a net importer from Canada but a net exporter to Mexico and Central America\Caribbean, though the Canadian and Mexican mills also compete in these markets as well, as does Russian rod and the South American mills. 

The development and location of the North American insulated wire and cable industry has naturally been hugely relevant for the US wirerod industry.  The entire industry has long been in structural decline, albeit with a business cycle superimposed upon it.  Consumers of OEM wires and cables (especially magnet wire, appliance wire and automotive wire) have increasingly migrated offshore to take advantage of cheap labour costs in Asia.  So these markets have shrunk significantly in North America with a result that some end use market segments such as automotive being supplied with finished wiring harnesses imported from Asia.  The clear outcome of the 2001/02 recession for the North American wire and cable industry was “cost reduction through globalisation”.  This had, and still has, significant implications for the industry – either relocate your production to where your customer is moving, or lose your customer, or outsource or offshore your production to Asia or Central America.  Air conditioning, home appliances, electric motors and automotive components were four copper end use sectors significantly impacted by this manufacturing revolution. 

The consequences for the wire and cable industry in North America were substantial.  Canadian production has suffered most through de-industrialisation, as its wire and cable industry was rationalised and production transferred to the fewer larger factories in the US and Mexico.  The US also suffered significantly, though the key regional trends were the movement of the wire and cable production from the North East and Mid West to the Southern US, and from the US into Mexico.  This relocation of rod consumers has favoured rod mills in south and western US and but has disadvantaged mills in the North East and Mid West.  The escalation of gasoline prices in the past two years has only served to accentuate this further. 

Phelps Dodge has long held the largest market position in the US wirerod industry and this continues under the new ownership of Freeport McMoran Copper and Gold.  Freeport McMoran has traditionally accounted for 50-55% of US rod production on an annual basis. Their share used to be a little lower at 40-45% while General Cable and Asarco were still active rod producers.  Following their exit from the market in 2004 and 2005, respectively, the then Phelps Dodge expanded production to fill the void, although as we have discussed imports also increased to supplement North American supply.  The importance of Freeport McMoran as an open market s

upplier has also increased substantially over this period both as their total output has increased, and also as their internal requirements have fallen. The motivation for Freeport McMoran’s ongoing involvement in the wirerod industry is clear - it is as a means of adding further value to its refined copper sales in North America. The downside of Freeport McMoran’s strong exposure to the US wirerod market is that with very limited viable export opportunities for rod and drawn wire, their future is irrevocably tied to the fortunes of the North American wire and cable industry which is in structural decline. But this does not mean that the outlook for Freeport McMoran’s wirerod business need be so as well. The company has demonstrated that it is possible to gain market share and volume in a declining market if your strategy is to be more efficient and outlast your competitors – akin to a last man standing approach. In this respect, the onset of a period of sustained high copper prices has been hugely beneficial to this policy if you aim to be a dedicated long term player in the copper wirerod business. General Cable and Asarco have exited the business and they will not be the only ones to do so. The working capital implications of high copper prices have compelled companies to examine their ongoing commitment to this business, and their decision as to whether to expand, maintain or reduce the volume of business that they do. Nexans have made it clear that they are actively reducing their involvement and any future closure of their Montreal plant would likely benefit Freeport McMoran’s existing mills in either Norwich, CT, or Chicago, IL, depending on the precise customer location. Superior Essex has also announced the planned permanent closure o

f its Vincennes, IA, Essex rod plant later this year as a result of the closure of its magnet wire plant at the same location.  It has also signalled a policy of decreasing its open market rod sales and is concentrating on rod production only for internal needs.  Its new overseas owner LS Cable Group might also have some ideas of its own. 

The delicate balance for Freeport McMoran and the North American rod industry as a whole is the risk of too many individual closures, market exits, or corporate policy decisions to only produce rod for internal group needs.  Reduced or constrained regional supply would soon be the trigger to reignite imports of Russian or Brazilian rod to the detriment of local production volume and pricing conditions, perhaps permanently.  Russian rod imports will inevitably resume at some point in the future in significant tonnages.  The North America rod industry will be working hard to ensure that it does not create the conditions for that to occur any time soon. Freeport McMoran operates a very large Contirod plant and a small Rautomead line at both of its facilities in El Paso, TX, and Norwich, CT.  In addition it has large Southwire lines in Chicago, IL, and Claypool, AZ.  Total production was 860,000 tonnes in 2007. 

The second ranked producer is Southwire with its own Southwire technology mill in Carrollton, GA.  As well as being a major supplier of copper and aluminium rod technology to the world market Southwire is a sizeable US rod producer and a significant manufacturer of building wire and power cables in the North American market.  The company remains family owned and has a strong tradition for hard work, efficiency, productivity and also to some extent secrecy.  That being said, the company cooperated as far as it was able to in the preparation of this report.  The company has achieved a consistent record of growth and expansion and has unquestionably benefited from the recent growth in the US building wire and power cable markets especially as the most rapid growth in US house construction has been in the south where it is headquartered.

This is also where labour rates are more competitive.  CRU estimates that Southwire produced 315,000 tonnes of wirerod in 2007, slightly down on 2006.  Production has been fairly stable in recent years.  A significant proportion of rod output is for captive in-house use for wire and cable production, though rod is also available for open market sale to third parties.  Having once been a copper producer Southwire’s future is clearly as a wire and cable manufacturer and SCR technology provider.  SCR is the dominant plant technology for copper wirerod production accounting for 46% of total world output in 2007.  Based on the project pipeline we expect that this share will rise above 50% over the course of the next few years. 

Superior Essex, now

owned by LS Cable Group of South Korea (which is itself a major copper rod and wire and cable producer in Asia) is the third ranked producer of wirerod in the US. Superior Essex has its origins in Superior Telecom (formerly a leading copper telecom cable manufacturer) and the Essex Group (formerly a significant magnet wire producer and also active in building wire).  The merger of these two dissimilar entities created Superior Essex but after prospering initially the company struggled in the depths of 2001/02 recession as sales dropped steeply in both of its core business lines and the company eventually had to declare Chapter 11 bankruptcy to clear its debts.  The company’s involvement in the wirerod business (based on its own, though now outdated, Essex technology) was solely to manufacture rod for internal group needs. 

Superior Essex’s participation as an open market supplier of rod in recent years has been the result of several factors.  Firstly and most importantly the erosion and migration of the US magnet wire business (to Mexico initially, and then offshore to China) has progressively left the company with surplus rod production capacity in Columbia City, IA, (2 plants) and Vincennes, IA, (one plant – now in phased closure) in locations geographically distant from where its magnet wire is now being produced (in Torreon, Mexico and Franklin, TN).  The decision to sell off its building wire operations in the emergence from Chapter 11 also removed a captive rod consumer from the group, although an agreement was reached on rod supply, which began the company’s external sales of rod.  Lately the high price of copper has accelerated substitution losses in copper telecom cable sales volumes to fibre optic, coaxial cable and wireless technologies.  This has also reduced captive needs.  These factors, coupled with the industry exits of General Cable and Asarco around this time, left Superior Essex after its emergence from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, with a significant volume of unutilised capacity at its four rod plants at a time when market demand was growing.  Crucially this was also at a time when the other major rod producers were operating at much higher rates of utilisation and so were collectively unable to pick up all of the slack themselves.  At that point the decision to expand production on under utilised production lines for the open market was an obvious one with prevailing copper prices at that time.  But of course only now with the benefit of hindsight can it be appreciated that the advent of $8,000/t copper and $140/barrel oil meant that this decision involved becoming involved in a poker game where bets were doubled for 3 years in a row. 

No one saw the copper price rally coming so it cannot be a criticism of Superior Essex’s actions at the time.  What it has done is to question its continuing involvement as an open market rod supplier in the future.  It is clear that the current management has decided that it is no longe

By the same token, the group’s financial and management resources were also required elsewhere to focus on their ambitious acquisition of Nexans global winding wire business and the integration of that into the Superior Essex manufacturing network. The acquisition of Superior Essex (which was openly for sale) by the LS Cable Group is somewhat curious. The two groups have few synergies and the logic for the acquisition is hard to find. Clearly the intention to create one of the world’s top 10 rod producers (as the combined output of the two companies will incidentally do) is not one of them. The buyout is wire and cable driven and it may be that the LS Cable Group’s vision is just to acquire a business in a growing global market place, or as a platform to sell their wire and cable production portfolio into the North American and European markets. Superior Essex did not choose to participate in our production survey (perhaps due to the acquisition above) but we estimate that their total rod production (for internal use and open market sale) increased from 149,000 tonnes in 2005 to 220,000 tonnes in 2007. 2008 sales will be much reduced, and it could be that this reduction may have contributed to the resumption in Russian rod imports this year. In 2007 70% of Superior Essex’s rod production was for internal use. The current strategy “… _is to increase the percentage of copper rod production suitable for internal use in the manufacture of magnet wire. To the extent that we are successful, our total copper rod production and our external sales of copper rod will decrease”._ Encore Wire is the next largest rod manufacturer in the USA. The company is a low cost manufacturer of copper building wire for residential and commercial applications. The company has an unequalled reputation for productivity and efficiency based around its single CRU International Limited confidential 3 - 20 Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Chapter 3 Production & Industry Trends product line (albeit with many variants in type) and when last benchmarked it was by a large margin the most productive wire and cable plant (sales per employee basis) in the world. The

company’s ethos is lean manufacturing with a small sales force exclusively servicing the distributor segment.  All of Encore Wire’s operations are based in a single facility in McKinney, TX, including its Southwire line which was installed in 2000 with a rated capacity of 98,000tpy. CRU estimates that its mill had been running at capacity recently, but that in 2007 it was run in excess of its rated capacity (at 111,000tpy), such was the strength of its commercial building wire business.  No rod is sold to external customers. 

Encore Wire produces copper rod at its own rod fabrication facility.  It produces copper rod from purchased copper cathodes and also reprocesses copper scrap generated by its operations and purchased scrap.  In 2007, the copper rod fabrication facility manufactured the majority of the company’s copper rod requirements.  All rod production is consumed internally though Encore Wire also makes supplementary purchases to meet all of its requirements for its insulated wire and cable production.  Encore Wire was a new entrant to the competitive US building wire market in 2000.  As its business model was based upon taking market share away from the existing players, its primary motivation for operating its own rod mill was to ensure security of supply, and to a lesser extent to guarantee rod quality suitable for its end use market. As a result of its aggressive business strategy, the company clearly came to the conclusion that it could not afford to be reliant upon external suppliers especially as one of these, Southwire, was the largest player in the building wire market.  The company’s strategy has been hugely successful growing from nothing at start up in 1989 to US$1.2bn annual sales in 2007, though this was admittedly bolstered by higher copper prices.  The company has prospered from the boom in residential and commercial construction across the US but especially in the south. Profitability has come under pressure recently as competition has intensified as building wire volumes stalled and have now started to decline. 

Amrod describes itself as a “leading independent copper rod producer in Northeastern USA.  Its plant is located in Port Newark, NJ, from where it has operated a mid-size Southwire line since 1984.  The company has no downstream insulated wire and cable interests and all its sales are to the open market.  Amrod manufactured 76,000 tonnes of rod in 2007, considerably above the 60,000 tonnes that it made in the previous two years.  The company appears to have benefited from the weak dollar that has caused Canadian exports to the US market to decline sharply, particularly in the NorthEastern states.  Amrod, as an independent open market supplier, stands to benefit from the withdrawal of Superior Essex as a major open market supplier and also from any potential future closure by Nexans in Canada. 

The remaining rod producers in the USA operate on a much smaller scale serving niche market sectors with particular r

equirements.  These mills include Sherburne Metal Products, which operates a 36,000tpy Outokumpu line in Rome, NY.  The mill offers oxygen free rod and drawn wire, tinned wire and some specialist alloys.  Output has been on a downward trend since 2000. Outokumpu Copper Nippert is part of Luvata, owned by the Nordic Capital Group.  It also operates a small outokumpu unit in Delaware, Ohio.  The facility manufactures rod, wire, profiles, welding electrodes with drawing and electrotinning lines.  United Copper Industries,

Wirerod production in **Mexico** has declined substantially from the impressive levels of 384,000 tonnes in 2000 and 352,000 tonnes in 2001 to below 300,000 tonnes for most of the remainder of the current decade.  2005 was the only year when output breached the 300,000 tonnes barrier to reach 318,000 tonnes as tightness in the US rod market following the closure of capacity at General Cable and Asarco.  This opportunity proved to be short lived as the rapid growth in Russian and Brazilian rod imports, coupled with the depreciating dollar quickly displaced Mexican exports.  Mexican exports of rod and drawn wire have fallen back to 40,000 to 50,000 tonnes in 2006/07. 

On the face of it, the migration of the Canadian and United States insulated wire and cable industry to Mexico and the southern US states would favour the Mexican mills from a logistical and freight perspective.  In reality, much of the relocation has centred on the magnet wire sector which requires superior quality rod for consistent fine wire drawing, without the problem of wire breaks.  Superior Essex have decided to rely on their own internal rod and drawn wire production, supplemented by external purchases from US rod mills.  Rea, with no in-house rod production, also favours US rod supply based on location and quality considerations (with Freeport McMoran the primary supplier).  The weakening US dollar has increased the attractiveness of US exports to Mexican maquiladora destinations, though freight costs are now of growing concern.  On balance, the southerly shift of the North American wire and cable industry should be favourable for the growth of Mexican rod production once the worst effects of the recession are over and when the exchange rate position normalises. The overwhelming impression in current market circumstances is that European rod premiums will continue to rise. #### **Cathode Premiums:** 

Cathode premiums are universally applied across Europe and without exception the European producers will apply and pass on the much published and widely recognised Chilean producer’s European cathode premium to their customers.  In 2007 for example, the producer’s cathode premium of US$125 per tonne was applied for pricing on the average LME basis, this was reduced to US$115 per tonne in 2008.  Pricing on the ‘Unknown’ LME basis is largely discouraged and there is no ‘official’ unknown producer premium but an additional supplement in the region of USD$50 is applied. 

The integrated refiner/rod producers therefore have a distinct advantage over their competitors in that they do not have to pay the producer’s cathode premium and on occasions have been known to discount their cathode premiums to generate spot rod sales.  The fact that European cathode producers firstly endorse and then apply the Chilean cathode premiums in Europe is a cause of some argument and discussion between cathode sellers and rod producers.  Suppliers from outside the territory such as the Russian and Egyptian producers do not usually distinguish the cathode premium, preferring to quote a single delivered premium over the LME Cash basis.

Payment terms as indicated above have been separated from the net premiums and identified. #### **Rod quality** 

The quality of the rod product is also important in determining the level of premium.  Some producers differentiate, brand and sell their rod products based on suitability for wiredrawing purposes.  Producers manufacture and then select their rod grades based on cathode input and manufacturing parameters.  Rod premiums vary according to grade with higher grades suitable for fine and multiwire applications sold at a premium.  Cumerio and Elektrokoppar for example produce two rod grades – one suitable for multiwire and fine wire applications and the other suitable for less exacting applications (telephone, power cables and suodronic wires). 

Imported rod from Russia are generally considered to be of inferior quality and suitable for nonfine application.  The lower rod premiums for Russian rod currently reflect this (notwithstanding issues about import duty).  With the likes of the major Russian producer UMMC applying (and currently undergoing tests) to register its cathode brand as LME deliverable and the likelihood that the other Russian producers will in time make similar applications, there should be no reason why these producers cannot be capable of producing rod qualities comparable to the European competitors.  If this were the case, premiums for Russian rods should increase and come more into line with the market. 

#### **Quantity** 

Quantity is important.  The general rule in the market is that the bigger the volum

e the greater the opportunity to negotiate lower premiums.  The biggest rod buyers such as Prysmian and Draka have huge buying leverage which they use to maximise premium advantage and exact the best terms.  But even the smaller buyers are clearly tuned in to market premiums with an invariably large number of potential suitor suppliers quoting for their business.  So they too can enjoy competitive premiums.

Also referred to as quotational period (QP) is a further option. Rod in Europe is generally sold on a QP based on the month of arrival.  For both buyers and producers, this is considered a neutral pricing period.  Historically, producers were able to flex the QP to gain commercial advantage.  They effectively were willing to give QP advantage to their customers in order to generate further business.  In times of historical market contango, allowing the customer to price during the month prior to the month of arrival was done at a relatively small cost.  In the recent and current context of wide market backwardations and huge structure volatility, QP flexibility is not an option and is not generally offered.

There is little published data on wirerod stock levels at rod mills, traders or rod consumers. Data is published on producer inventories of rod in the USA, South Korea, Japan and Taiwan but not for anywhere else. Faced with this paucity of data, we have decided not to include data on stock levels or changes for any country, so that country by country comparisons can be made on the same basis for any year or period of years.  Annual stock changes appear to be minimal in most cases and especially so in relation to the size of the total market.  Our year to year consumption calculations therefore include an element of either stock building or stock drawdown based on the precise conditions prevailing at that time. 

The only exceptions we have made to this are where the stock changes have been so large as to <u>materially affect consumption in one year or over several years.  The stock changes that we</u> have included are all related to the effects of Russian wirerod on the global market.  The first example of this is in the Netherland in 2004 and 2005.  Trade statistics reveal that Russia exported significant volumes of rod in the final quarter of 2004 via the Netherlands en route to their ultimate destination. A more protracted problem appears to exist with Russia. ## 3.4 Company Production Rankings 

#### 3.4.1 Methodology 

The copper wirerod company production totals have been calculated on the following basis: Company production totals for each mill on a calendar year basis, reflecting the equity ownership stake that they have in each mill, or joint venture, multiplied by the percentage of that year that they had that equity interest. 

Thus in the most complicated case, for Freeport McMoran Copper & Gold’s attributable copper wirerod production in 2007, the basis of the total is as follows: - 

Freeport McMoran Copper & Gold’s US rod production (100% owned) 

#### **+** 

Equity ownership shares of company by company rod production totals in the overseas subsidiaries (Chile, Zambia, Philippines, Thailand) of Phelps Dodge International Corporation, multiplied by 75% (General Cable’s acquisition of these assets occurred in September 2007) 

#### **=** 

Freeport McMoran Copper & Gold’s total attributable copper wirerod production. 

#### **Company production totals have been identified/estimated from the following sources:-** 

- 1) Published company data, adjusted for calendar basis, e.g. from annual report 

- 2) Direct CRU wirerod survey return (email, fax, phone or visit) 

- 3) Estimations by competing mills operating in that country/region 

- 4) Estimation by CRU, reconciled with other returns to country production total 

- 5) Estimation by CRU based on refined consumption, trade flows or mill capacity 

We would like to thank all the companies that participated in the survey.  This enabled us to identify company production totals for over 85% of all mills producing at least 50,000tpy.  This cooperation greatly increased the accuracy of the overall production survey. CRU

acknowledges that the data is not definitive, but that we will attempt to improve the accuracy further in 2009. In this regard we greatly welcome customer feedback to <u>jon.barnes@crugroup.com.</u> 

#### 3.4.2 Main Findings – Selected Highlights (Tables 3.20 & 3.21) 

- **Freeport McMoran Copper & Gold (formerly Phelps Dodge) has been the world’s leading rod manufacturer for the last three years.  US output has been falling.** 

- **Freeport McMoran’s overseas rod equity joint ventures were sold to General Cable in September 2007.  This cuts attributable production from 2008 onwards.** 

- **Nexans was ranked #2 worldwide, but output has been in decline (voluntarily to some extent, but also market related) in Canada and France.  Germany stable.** 

- **Cumerio was #3 in 2007; Norddeutsche Affinerie was #4 in 2007.  The merger between the two creates a new world leader in the copper rod business.**
